lesson.title: Taming the Beast: How Feedback Turns Wild Gain into a Precise Number
lesson.summary: Closed-loop gain is the overall gain of an amplifier once negative feedback routes a fraction of the output back to the input, and for a real op-amp it converges to a value set almost entirely by the feedback network rather than by the amplifier's own unpredictable open-loop gain.
lesson.body:
The previous two chapters left off with a real problem: open-loop gain is enormous and unpredictable, yet an ideal op-amp is assumed to have infinite gain, which sounds like it should make the problem worse rather than better. The resolution is negative feedback: a portion of the output signal is fed back and subtracted from the input, and this feedback loop is what converts a wild, barely controllable open-loop gain into a precise, repeatable closed-loop gain.

Let beta (β) represent the feedback fraction, the portion of the output signal that is routed back to subtract from the input. The standard result relating closed-loop gain A_CL to open-loop gain A_OL and feedback fraction beta is A_CL = A_OL / (1 + A_OL times beta). This formula looks like it still depends heavily on the unpredictable A_OL, but the dependence weakens dramatically as A_OL grows large, which is exactly the regime real op-amps operate in.

Take A_OL = 200,000, a realistic open-loop gain, with a feedback network that returns 1 percent of the output, so beta = 0.01. Plugging in: A_CL = 200,000 / (1 + 200,000 times 0.01) = 200,000 / (1 + 2000) = 200,000 / 2001, which works out to approximately 99.95. Compare that to 1 / beta = 1 / 0.01 = 100. The two values differ by only about 0.05, less than a tenth of one percent.

That near-perfect agreement is the whole point. As A_OL grows, the term A_OL times beta in the denominator dominates the 1, so A_CL approaches A_OL / (A_OL times beta), and the A_OL terms cancel, leaving A_CL approaching 1 / beta. In the limit of infinite open-loop gain, exactly the ideal op-amp assumption from the last chapter, the closed-loop gain becomes exactly 1 / beta, completely independent of A_OL. Since beta is set by a network of external resistors, which can be manufactured to a tight, known tolerance (often 1 percent or better), the closed-loop gain becomes a precise, designer-chosen number rather than an unpredictable property of the amplifier itself.

This is the deep reason the ideal op-amp assumption of infinite open-loop gain is not just a convenient fiction but an accurate one: once negative feedback is present, the amplifier's actual open-loop gain barely matters, provided it is large enough (a loop gain, A_OL times beta, of a few thousand is typically enough to make the approximation excellent, as the example above shows). What remains to explain is what this convergence looks like physically at the op-amp's two input pins, which is exactly the subject of the next chapter, the virtual short.
